title: Finite Automata
tagline: DFA and NFA — the simplest machines that can recognise patterns, accept strings, and lay the mathematical foundation for every lexer ever written.

sections.content:
Every time you type a search query, compile source code, or validate an email address, a tiny mathematical machine is silently running underneath. That machine is a **finite automaton** — one of the oldest and most elegant ideas in theoretical computer science, dating to the 1950s work of Stephen Kleene, Michael Rabin, and Dana Scott. Despite being half a century old, it is also one of the most practically useful: every regular expression engine, every programming-language lexer, and every network protocol state machine is, at its core, a finite automaton.

A **finite automaton** is an abstract machine defined by a finite set of *states*, a set of *transitions* that move between states in response to input symbols, a single designated *start state*, and one or more *accept states*. You feed it an input string one character at a time; if the machine lands on an accept state when the input is exhausted, it *accepts* the string — declaring it a member of the language the machine recognises. Otherwise it *rejects*.

There are two fundamental flavours. A **Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA)** has exactly one transition per (state, input-symbol) pair — no ambiguity, no choice, purely mechanical. A **Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA)** relaxes this: a state may have zero, one, or *many* transitions on the same symbol, plus special **epsilon (ε) transitions** that move between states without consuming any input. NFAs look more powerful, but they are not: every NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA. Both recognise exactly the same class of languages — the **regular languages** — and neither can recognise anything outside that class.

This chapter builds the full picture from scratch: formal definitions, worked examples, the NFA-to-DFA conversion via subset construction, DFA minimisation, Thompson's construction from regular expressions, real-world applications, complexity implications, and the limits of what these machines can do.

sections.title: Turnstiles, Traffic Lights, and Choose-Your-Own-Adventure Books
sections.content:
A **DFA** is best understood as a **subway turnstile**. At any moment the turnstile is in exactly one physical state: locked or unlocked. Insert a valid token and it moves to the unlocked state; push through and it returns to locked. There is no ambiguity, no memory of history beyond the current state, and no 'maybe' transitions. The machine is a pure function: given the current state and one input event, it produces exactly one next state.

An **NFA** is like a **choose-your-own-adventure book** where the reader is allowed to split into multiple simultaneous copies. Each time the story offers a choice, every copy follows a different branch in parallel. The 'machine' accepts if *any* copy of the reader reaches a happy ending. In computation, we simulate this by tracking the *set* of all states any copy could currently be in — which is precisely the idea behind subset construction. The NFA's non-determinism is an abstraction that makes design easy; subset construction converts it back to something a real machine can execute.

A **traffic light controller** illustrates why *state matters*: green → yellow → red → green. The same input (a timer tick) means different things depending on which state you are in. The controller has no memory of *how many* cars passed, no stack, no counters — just the current colour. That is the power and the limitation of finite automata: they can track *which phase* they are in, but not *how many times* something happened.

sections.title: Formal Definition: What a DFA Actually Is
sections.content:
A **DFA** is a 5-tuple **(Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F)** where:

- **Q** is a finite, non-empty set of *states*
- **Σ** is a finite *alphabet* of input symbols
- **δ: Q × Σ → Q** is the *transition function* — for every state and every symbol, it specifies exactly one next state
- **q₀ ∈ Q** is the *start state*
- **F ⊆ Q** is the set of *accept states* (also called final states)

The transition function δ is *total*: it must be defined for every (state, symbol) pair. If a real problem has no sensible transition for some pair, we add a special **dead state** (or *trap state*) that all undefined transitions point to, and from which no transition leads to an accept state.

To **run** a DFA on input string w = a₁a₂…aₙ: start in q₀, then iteratively apply δ — the state after reading the first i symbols is δ(δ(…δ(q₀, a₁)…, aᵢ₋₁), aᵢ). When the input is exhausted, the machine accepts if the current state is in F, and rejects otherwise.

The set of all strings a DFA M accepts is called the **language of M**, written L(M). A language is called *regular* if some DFA recognises it. This definition is tight: there exist languages — like {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0}, balanced parentheses, or palindromes — that *cannot* be recognised by any DFA, no matter how many states you add. The formal proof uses the **Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages**.

sections.caption: DFA accepting all strings over {a,b} that contain 'ab' as a substring. q0 = no progress, q1 = last symbol was 'a', q2 = 'ab' seen (accept). Every state has exactly one outgoing arrow per symbol.

sections.title: Walking Through a DFA: A Worked Example
sections.content:
Let us trace the DFA that accepts strings containing the substring `ab` (shown in the diagram above) on the input `bab`:

1. Start in **q0**. Read `b` → δ(q0, b) = q0. Stay in q0.
2. In **q0**. Read `a` → δ(q0, a) = q1. Move to q1.
3. In **q1**. Read `b` → δ(q1, b) = q2. Move to q2.
4. Input exhausted. q2 ∈ F → **ACCEPT**.

Now trace the string `ba`:
1. Start in **q0**. Read `b` → q0.
2. In **q0**. Read `a` → q1.
3. Input exhausted. q1 ∉ F → **REJECT**.

And the empty string ε:
1. Start in **q0**. No input. q0 ∉ F → **REJECT**.

Notice that the DFA needs only three states to capture an infinite language — all strings containing `ab`. This is the beauty of finite automata: a finite machine compactly encodes an infinite set of strings by tracking *progress* rather than *history*. The state tells you everything you need to know about past input that is relevant to future acceptance — nothing more, nothing less. This minimal sufficient summary of past input is exactly what the **Myhill-Nerode theorem** formalises.

sections.title: Non-deterministic Finite Automata: Embracing Ambiguity
sections.content:
An **NFA** is also a 5-tuple **(Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F)**, but the transition function changes character: **δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → P(Q)**, where P(Q) is the *power set* of Q (the set of all subsets of Q). For any state and any symbol (including ε), δ returns a *set* of next states — possibly empty, possibly containing many states.

The **ε-transition** (epsilon transition) is a move the machine can make without consuming any input symbol. ε-transitions are pure bookkeeping — they allow NFA fragments to be connected together without requiring an input symbol at the joint. The **ε-closure** of a state q, written ε-closure(q), is the set of all states reachable from q via zero or more ε-transitions.

An NFA **accepts** a string if there *exists at least one* computational path through the machine's choices that leads to an accept state after consuming the entire input. Equivalently: simulate all paths simultaneously; accept if any path ends in an accept state.

Why bother with NFAs if DFAs are cleaner? Because **NFAs are dramatically easier to construct from a specification**. A regular expression maps to an NFA in a simple, mechanical, fragment-by-fragment way (Thompson's construction). The resulting NFA may have many ε-transitions and non-deterministic branches, but it is structurally transparent. Converting that NFA to a DFA (via subset construction) is a separate mechanical step. The separation keeps each step simple.

sections.caption: NFA accepting strings ending in 'abb'. s0 non-deterministically 'guesses' when the suffix begins — on reading 'a' it can stay in s0 or jump to s1. An equivalent DFA requires 8 states.

sections.title: Subset Construction: Converting NFA to DFA
sections.content:
The **subset construction** (also called the *powerset construction*) is the algorithm that converts any NFA into an equivalent DFA. The key insight: the DFA's states are *sets* of NFA states — each DFA state represents all the NFA states the machine could simultaneously be in.

**Algorithm outline:**

1. Compute the ε-closure of the NFA's start state q₀. This set is the DFA's start state.
2. For each DFA state S (a set of NFA states) and each input symbol a ∈ Σ:
   - Compute MOVE(S, a) = ∪ { δ_NFA(q, a) | q ∈ S } — all NFA states reachable in one a-step from any state in S.
   - Compute ε-closure(MOVE(S, a)) — expand ε-transitions.
   - This result is the DFA's next state for (S, a).
3. A DFA state S is an accept state if S ∩ F_NFA ≠ ∅ — if *any* NFA accept state is in S.
4. Repeat for all newly discovered DFA states until no new states appear.

**Worst case:** An NFA with n states can produce a DFA with up to **2ⁿ states** (one for each subset of Q). In practice, the reachable subsets are usually far fewer. But adversarial examples do exist — the canonical one is the NFA for 'strings where the n-th-from-last symbol is `a`': it has n+1 states but the minimal DFA has 2ⁿ states.

**Why this proves DFA = NFA in power:** The subset construction always terminates and always produces a correct DFA. Therefore, for every NFA there exists an equivalent DFA. The converse is trivially true (every DFA is a special NFA with |δ(q,a)| = 1 for all q, a). Hence DFAs and NFAs accept precisely the same class of languages.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The DFA simulator tracks a single integer state — O(n) time, O(1) extra space. The NFA simulator tracks a Set of active states, implementing subset construction on-the-fly. Each input symbol fans out all transitions from the current set and unions the results. Both run in O(n) time in the input length; the NFA version additionally scales with |Q| per step because set operations touch each state at most once.

sections.title: Thompson's Construction: From Regex to NFA
sections.content:
**Thompson's construction** (1968) converts a regular expression to an NFA with ε-transitions in a systematic, bottom-up way. Each regex operator maps to a fixed NFA *fragment* with exactly one start state and one accept state. Fragments are wired together using ε-transitions.

The four base cases:

**Single symbol `a`:** Two states — q_start, q_accept — with one transition on `a`. This is the atom.

**Concatenation r·s:** Take NFA(r) and NFA(s). Add an ε-transition from r's accept state to s's start state. The result has r's start as the new start and s's accept as the new accept.

**Union r|s:** Create a new start state with ε-transitions to both NFA(r) and NFA(s). Create a new accept state with ε-transitions from both NFA(r) and NFA(s). Either branch may be taken.

**Kleene star r\*:** Create a new start state and a new accept state. Add ε-transitions: new-start → NFA(r).start, NFA(r).accept → new-accept, NFA(r).accept → NFA(r).start (the loop back), and new-start → new-accept (the zero-repetitions path).

The resulting NFA has at most **2n states** (at most two states per symbol or operator in the regex). It may look tangled with ε-transitions, but it is structurally guaranteed to be correct. The subsequent subset construction then eliminates the ε-transitions and non-determinism, producing a runnable DFA. This two-step pipeline — Thompson's then subset construction — is precisely what tools like `lex`, `flex`, and the Rust `regex` crate implement at compile time.

flowchart LR
  A["new start"] -- "ε" --> B["NFA(r) start"]
  A -- "ε" --> C["NFA(s) start"]
  B -- "..." --> D["NFA(r) accept"]
  C -- "..." --> E["NFA(s) accept"]
  D -- "ε" --> F["new accept"]
  E -- "ε" --> F
sections.caption: Thompson's construction fragment for union r|s. The new start ε-branches into both sub-NFAs; both sub-NFA accepts ε-merge into the new accept.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Each builder function creates at most two new states and a few ε-edges. Concatenating k operators creates at most 2k states total — Thompson's construction is linear in the size of the regex. The fragment approach makes the algorithm compositional: build small correct pieces, wire them together. No regex parsing heuristics needed.

sections.title: DFA Minimisation: Hopcroft's Algorithm
sections.content:
After subset construction you have a correct DFA, but it may have redundant states — two states that behave identically on all future input and can be merged without changing the accepted language. **Hopcroft's algorithm** (1971) finds the unique **minimal DFA** for a given regular language in O(n log n) time (where n is the number of states).

The algorithm works by *partition refinement*:

1. Start with two groups: accept states F and non-accept states Q \ F.
2. Repeatedly *refine* the partition: two states p and q are in the same group only if, for *every* input symbol a, δ(p, a) and δ(q, a) land in the *same* group. If this fails for some symbol, split the group.
3. Repeat until no further splits occur. The resulting groups are the **equivalence classes** of indistinguishable states.
4. Merge each equivalence class into a single state. The resulting DFA is minimal.

**Why minimal?** The **Myhill-Nerode theorem** provides the theoretical foundation. Two strings x and y are *Myhill-Nerode equivalent* with respect to language L if for every suffix z: xz ∈ L iff yz ∈ L. The number of equivalence classes equals the number of states in the minimal DFA. This theorem simultaneously proves minimality (the Hopcroft DFA achieves the lower bound) and the Pumping Lemma (if L has infinitely many classes, no finite automaton can recognise it).

For the `ab`-substring language: the three states q0, q1, q2 are already minimal. You cannot merge any pair, because each state is distinguishable from the others by some suffix: q0 is distinguished from q1 by `b` (q0+`b` = reject, q1+`b` = accept); q1 is distinguished from q2 by ε (q1 rejects ε, q2 accepts ε).

flowchart TD

{q2} vs {q0, q1}"] --> B["Can q0 and q1 be merged?
Check: on 'b'
δ(q0,b)=q0 non-accept
δ(q1,b)=q2 accept"]
  B --> C["Different groups → split!
{q2}, {q1}, {q0}"]
  C --> D["No further splits possible
Minimal DFA: 3 states"]
sections.caption: Hopcroft's partition refinement trace for the 'contains ab' DFA. The initial accept/non-accept split, then the distinguishing 'b' transition reveals q0 and q1 must be separate states.

sections.title: What Regular Languages Can and Cannot Do
sections.content:
The class of regular languages has clean closure properties. If L₁ and L₂ are regular, then so are:
- **Union** L₁ ∪ L₂ (run both DFAs in parallel, accept if either accepts)
- **Intersection** L₁ ∩ L₂ (product construction)
- **Complement** Σ\* \ L (flip accept and non-accept states in the minimal DFA)
- **Concatenation** L₁·L₂ and **Kleene star** L₁\*
- **Reversal** L^R

These closure properties make regular languages extremely well-behaved and easy to compose. You can build complex pattern matchers by combining simpler ones, and the result is always still regular.

However, regular languages **cannot** do counting. They cannot recognise:
- **Balanced parentheses** — {(ⁿ)ⁿ | n ≥ 0} requires counting depth, which needs unbounded memory
- **Palindromes** — abaⁿbⁿ type patterns require remembering arbitrary amounts of past input
- **Equal counts** — {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 1} is the classic example

The **Pumping Lemma** is the tool used to prove a language is *not* regular. It says: if L is regular, there is a pumping length p such that any string w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be split into w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1, and xyzⁱ ∈ L for all i ≥ 0. The string y can be 'pumped' up or down while staying in the language. If you can find a string where no such split works, L is not regular.

To recognise counting languages you need a **pushdown automaton** (with a stack — recognises context-free languages) or a **Turing machine** (with unbounded tape). Understanding the limits of finite automata is as important as understanding their strengths.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The product construction runs two DFAs in lockstep using a pair of states, accepting only when both reach accept states. This works for intersection; for union, accept when *either* is in an accept state. For complement, swap accept and non-accept in the minimal DFA. The balanced-AB function shows why counting needs more power than a DFA — it uses an integer counter that can grow without bound.

sections.title: Real-World Applications: Where Finite Automata Live
sections.content:
Finite automata are not textbook curiosities — they are workhorse infrastructure in production software.

**Lexers and compilers:** The first phase of compilation is *lexical analysis* — splitting source text into tokens (keywords, identifiers, numbers, operators). Each token class is described by a regular expression; the lexer generator (`lex`, `flex`, ANTLR's lexer) converts them all into a single combined DFA. Every subsequent `nextToken()` call runs the DFA in O(1) amortised per character. This is why lexing is the fastest phase of compilation.

**Regex engines:** Libraries like Python's `re`, JavaScript's built-in regex, and Java's `Pattern` compile patterns into NFAs and simulate them. The critical distinction is *how*: PCRE-style engines use **backtracking NFA simulation**, which can be exponential on adversarial input. Google's **RE2** library and Rust's **`regex` crate** use true DFA simulation (or lazy DFA construction), guaranteeing O(n) time at the cost of rejecting some PCRE features like backreferences that are not regular.

**Network protocols:** TCP's connection state machine (CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED) is a finite automaton. HTTP/2 stream states, TLS handshake steps, and Bluetooth pairing protocols are all modelled as state machines — the automaton formalism ensures every transition is explicit and every edge case is considered.

**Search engines and grep:** GNU `grep` with `-E` (extended regex) and `ripgrep` compile patterns to DFAs for O(n) substring search across files. The Boyer-Moore algorithm used in non-regex search is also essentially a pre-computed DFA over pattern prefixes.

**Hardware design:** Digital circuits are finite state machines implemented directly in logic gates. An elevator controller, a vending machine, a USB interface chip — all are finite automata with states encoded in flip-flop registers and transitions encoded in combinational logic.

**A note on catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS):** Many production security incidents have exploited the exponential behaviour of backtracking regex engines. The attack is called **ReDoS** (Regular Expression Denial of Service). A carefully crafted input string can cause a backtracking engine to explore exponentially many paths before concluding a non-match, stalling a web server for seconds or minutes on a single request. The fix is to use an engine with guaranteed O(n) behaviour (RE2, Rust regex), or to audit your patterns for *ambiguous quantifiers* — nested `(a+)+` style patterns that the Pumping Lemma would immediately flag as exponentially backtracking. Understanding the NFA-vs-DFA distinction is the prerequisite for understanding why this attack exists.

**Interview and exam insights:** The most common finite automata questions test whether you can (1) draw a DFA for a given language description, (2) trace a DFA/NFA on a given input, (3) apply the Pumping Lemma to prove a language is not regular, and (4) explain subset construction. Key facts to have cold: DFA and NFA are equivalent in power; subset construction can blow up to 2ⁿ states; the minimal DFA is unique; Thompson's construction builds an NFA in O(|regex|) states; DFAs cannot count (no {aⁿbⁿ}). Also know: `(a+)+` is a ReDoS footgun in backtracking engines but perfectly O(n) in RE2/Rust regex — this bridges theory to practical security knowledge.

items: A **DFA** (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) has exactly one transition per (state, symbol) pair — total, deterministic, runs in O(n) time per string of length n.
An **NFA** allows zero-or-many transitions per symbol plus ε-transitions; it accepts if *any* computational path reaches an accept state.
**DFA and NFA are equivalent in expressive power** — both recognise exactly the regular languages; every NFA converts to a DFA via subset construction, with at most 2ⁿ states in the worst case.

**Thompson's construction** converts a regular expression to an NFA with ε-transitions in O(|regex|) states; **subset construction** then converts the NFA to a DFA; **Hopcroft's algorithm** minimises the DFA to its unique smallest form.
Regular languages are **closed** under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, and Kleene star — they compose cleanly.
**Finite automata cannot count**: languages like {aⁿbⁿ}, balanced parentheses, or palindromes require a pushdown automaton or Turing machine; the Pumping Lemma proves the impossibility.
**ReDoS attacks** exploit exponential backtracking in NFA-simulating regex engines; engines that run true DFA simulation (RE2, Rust regex) guarantee O(n) time regardless of pattern.

quiz.question: What is the formal definition of a DFA's transition function?
options: δ: Q × Σ → P(Q), mapping each (state, symbol) pair to a set of next states
δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → Q, allowing epsilon transitions
δ: Q × Σ → Q, mapping each (state, symbol) pair to exactly one next state
δ: Q × Σ → F, always mapping to an accept state
quiz.explanation: In a DFA the transition function δ: Q × Σ → Q is total and deterministic — for every combination of state and input symbol it returns exactly one next state. This distinguishes it from an NFA whose transition function returns a set of states.

quiz.question: An NFA has 5 states. What is the maximum number of states the equivalent DFA produced by subset construction could have?
quiz.explanation: Subset construction tracks subsets of NFA states. With 5 NFA states there are 2⁵ = 32 possible subsets. In practice the reachable subsets are usually far fewer, but 32 is the worst-case upper bound.

quiz.question: An NFA accepts a string if:
options: Every possible computational path ends in an accept state.
At least one computational path ends in an accept state after consuming all input.
The start state is also an accept state.
No dead states are reached during any computation.
quiz.explanation: Non-determinism means the machine explores multiple paths simultaneously. Acceptance requires only that *at least one* of those paths terminates in an accept state after the full input is consumed. All-paths acceptance would be a different (co-NFA) model.

quiz.question: What does an ε-transition do in an NFA?
options: It transitions to the dead (trap) state when no symbol matches.
It allows the automaton to move to a new state without consuming any input symbol.
It marks the current state as a final accept state.
It resets the automaton to the start state.
quiz.explanation: An ε-transition (epsilon transition) is a state change that consumes no input. It is used extensively in Thompson's construction to wire NFA fragments together without needing an input symbol at the junction, and its reachable set is computed as the ε-closure.

quiz.question: Which algorithm converts a regular expression directly into an NFA with ε-transitions?
options: Subset construction
Hopcroft's minimisation
Thompson's construction
Earley's parsing algorithm
quiz.explanation: Thompson's construction (1968) maps each regex operator (symbol, concatenation, union, Kleene star) to a small NFA fragment connected by ε-transitions, building the NFA bottom-up from the regex parse tree. The result has at most 2×|regex| states.

quiz.question: Which of the following languages CANNOT be recognised by any finite automaton?
options: All strings over {a,b} containing 'ab' as a substring
All strings over {a,b} of even length
All strings of the form aⁿbⁿ where n ≥ 1
All strings over {a,b} ending in 'abb'
quiz.explanation: aⁿbⁿ requires counting n — unbounded memory. A finite automaton has only a fixed finite set of states, so it cannot track arbitrarily large counts. The Pumping Lemma formally proves this language is not regular. The other three languages are regular and each has a straightforward DFA.

quiz.question: What is the role of Hopcroft's algorithm in the regex-to-DFA pipeline?
options: It converts a regular expression into an NFA with ε-transitions.
It converts an NFA into a DFA by tracking sets of NFA states.
It minimises a DFA by merging indistinguishable states into equivalence classes.
It checks whether two DFAs accept the same language.
quiz.explanation: Hopcroft's algorithm (1971) performs partition refinement on DFA states. It starts by separating accept from non-accept states, then repeatedly splits groups when states within a group behave differently on some input symbol. The final groups are the equivalence classes of indistinguishable states, which are merged to form the unique minimal DFA.

quiz.question: Why do some regex engines exhibit exponential running time on certain inputs?
options: They use true DFA simulation, which requires building the full power-set of states.
They use backtracking NFA simulation, which can explore exponentially many computational paths.
Regular expressions can describe non-regular languages when lookaheads are added.
Unicode normalisation adds exponential overhead to character comparisons.
quiz.explanation: Backtracking NFA engines (like PCRE) explore one path, and when it fails they back up and try another. Adversarial patterns — e.g. (a+)+ — can cause exponential path explosion on non-matching inputs. This is the ReDoS attack. Engines that run true DFA simulation (RE2, Rust regex) guarantee O(n) by never backtracking.

quiz.question: The Myhill-Nerode theorem states that the number of states in the minimal DFA for a language L equals:
options: The number of symbols in the alphabet Σ
The length of the longest string in L
The number of equivalence classes of the Myhill-Nerode relation on Σ*
Two raised to the power of the number of NFA states
quiz.explanation: The Myhill-Nerode theorem defines an equivalence relation on Σ*: strings x and y are equivalent if for every suffix z, xz ∈ L iff yz ∈ L. The number of equivalence classes is exactly the number of states in the minimal DFA. This simultaneously proves minimality and, when the classes are infinite, proves the language is not regular.

quiz.question: If language L₁ is regular and L₂ is regular, which of the following is guaranteed to also be regular?
options: L₁ raised to the power of L₂
The set of all strings NOT in L₁ (complement of L₁)
The set of all context-free extensions of L₁
The language obtained by removing all ε-transitions from L₁
quiz.explanation: Regular languages are closed under complement: given the minimal DFA for L₁, swapping accept and non-accept states produces a DFA for the complement. Regular languages are also closed under union, intersection, concatenation, Kleene star, and reversal — this closure makes them very composable.
